name: Release timeline
summary: This page: every shipped and planned feature with its date, admin only.

name: Standalone JLPT study
summary: The JLPT route refused the whole request without a WaniKani token, although the token was only ever used for the progress overlay - the kanji themselves come from a table WaniKani has no part in. So a member who had not connected could not read the JLPT data at all, only the part of it that was about them. The token is required where it is used and nowhere else now: the kanji stand on their own, and the overlay is simply empty without one.

name: Optional WaniKani connection
summary: An account no longer requires WaniKani. The six connection fields are nullable, and every surface that used them now asks whether a connection exists instead of assuming one - WaniKani-derived boards leave unconnected accounts out rather than ranking them at level zero.

name: Capability gating
summary: One capability map decides what a member without WaniKani sees, hides or finds disabled.

name: WaniKani-free game pool
summary: The games drew only from an account's own WaniKani assignments, so a player who had never connected had a pool of nothing: Match and Shiritori answered "Only 0 eligible items are available" while the lobby offered them and the welcome copy promised them by name. The subjects were never personal - they are the shared catalogue, which Daily Challenge has always played straight off - so assignments are treated as a filter rather than the source, and a player without a connection draws the catalogue up to level ten. Not the whole of it: sixty levels of vocabulary is a dictionary rather than a game. A connected player is untouched, since every existing account has assignments and the fallback never fires for them.

name: Connect your WaniKani account
summary: A page that explains what connecting unlocks and walks through adding the token.

name: Open Google sign-up

name: Developer and Advanced modes
summary: Two global mode flags, toggled from the flags page; the footer wears DEV and ADV chips while they are on.

name: Timestamps and the Shelved tab
summary: Releases carry their real commit instant - John's point: a timestamp beats sort cleverness - and backlogged or killed work stays visible on its own tab.

name: Manage accounts redesign
summary: Each account row keeps one visible Open-as-user action and folds the rest into a compact overflow menu.

name: Trouble and Favourites, visible from Study
summary: The queue tag filter now shows as a chip you can clear, so a sticky Trouble filter no longer hides most of the due reviews without saying so, and the Trouble & favourites lists open from the Study page rather than only the game lobby, History and the JLPT explorer.

name: Your Lists cards match the shared card
summary: Subject cards put the level in the top-right corner the way every other surface does, and the remove button moves to the bottom-right instead of squatting where the level belongs.

name: Grouped header navigation
summary: The header drops from eleven flat items wrapping onto two rows to eight groups on one. Explore holds the three explorers, Progress holds History and Stats, Read holds Read and News, and Settings holds Libraries.

name: Release names show kana and kanji
summary: The release name prints its kana reading beside the kanji instead of hiding the kanji in a tooltip, so both scripts are readable at a glance.

name: Version number opens the release timeline
summary: For an admin the footer version number and the header motto link straight to the release timeline. Everyone else still sees them as plain text, since the page is admin-only.

name: Maps for Japan, the US and Canada
summary: Map data now covers 47 Japanese prefectures, 51 US states and 13 Canadian provinces and territories, each with capital, largest city, population, area and regional metadata, rebuilt reproducibly by the map:build scripts.

name: Study queue as a list
summary: The Study queue offers the same grid/list toggle the tagged lists and history already use, so a long queue can be scanned one line at a time. The choice is remembered per surface.

name: Geo dataset under test
summary: The map data the capital, country and size games will read is now pinned by tests: region counts, unique ids, a capital and a positive population and area for all 111 divisions, and the comparison helpers.

name: Reserved map ids for all three countries
summary: US states and Canadian provinces get their own reserved subject-id bands beside the prefectures, so map rounds for any country can ride the existing run tables. Japan keeps the exact ids recorded runs already hold.

name: One distractor rule for every map
summary: What makes a convincing wrong answer on a map - neighbours first, then region, then proximity - moves out of the Japan question builder so states and provinces use the same rule. Japan scores exactly as before.

name: School Grade explorer
summary: Kanji by Japanese school year, with the on and kun readings approved for that grade rather than every reading the character has. Covers grades 1 to 6, secondary joyo and jinmeiyo, searchable and paged.

name: Public updates page
summary: Shipped releases are public at /releases, grouped by month and expandable for the detail. Four entries that described a fixed security weakness precisely carry a cleansed public wording; the admin timeline keeps the honest text and the planned work.

name: Search across every catalogue
summary: A search box in the header and a results page that asks WaniKani, JLPT and School Grades at once, ranked into one list with exact characters and meanings first. Filter to a single catalogue with the source pills.

name: One level pill everywhere
summary: Reported by John: the level read as a pill in the lists and as faint borderless text on the study card and in the view modal. The in-glyph level and success rate are pills everywhere now.

name: Modals hold one height
summary: Reported by John: modals grew and shrank with their contents. ModalShell now owns two heights, a content one for forms and a fixed one for lists, and a test fails if a modal hand-rolls its own again.

name: Search results open where they live
summary: A search result now opens the explorer that holds it with the search already applied. Signed-out visitors keep the results as a lookup rather than being offered links that would bounce off the sign-in wall.

name: Quiz yourself on grade readings
summary: The grade grid hides its readings on request so the same page becomes a self-test: see the kanji, say the on and kun readings, select the card to check. Nothing is recorded, which is the point - it is the rehearsal, not the exam.

name: Search keeps its place on a phone
summary: The header search field cost about 150px on a phone and the mobile nav clips rather than wraps, so it had silently pushed the Admin link off the end of the row. On a phone it is now the icon alone, linking to the search page.

name: Stop showing compound-only readings
summary: Reported by John: the grade cards listed readings a character never has on its own. KANJIDIC hyphenates compound-only forms, and 31 of the 80 first-grade entries carried one, so the King card claimed a kun reading of -nou that only exists inside a compound. Those are filtered out of the display.

name: Animated stroke order
summary: Every kanji can be watched being written, one stroke at a time, with optional stroke numbers. Stroke data comes from KanjiVG under CC BY-SA, credited on every animation, and is rebuilt reproducibly from a pinned commit with pnpm strokes:build. Covers all 2,899 school-grade characters.

name: Compare the printed kanji with the strokes
summary: The stroke-order view shows the printed character beside the animation, so a child copying strokes has the real shape to compare against, with the grade, JLPT and WaniKani levels, frequency rank and readings underneath.

name: Official readings from the joyo table
summary: Reported by John: the grade cards listed every reading a character has ever taken. They now use the readings from the joyo table, which is the cabinet-notified list for general use - so King correctly shows no kun reading, Sound files its in reading as on, and Life drops from twenty-one readings to ten. Both fonts are shown in the stroke view for comparison.

name: Stroke order beyond the grades page
summary: Stroke order moves into a shared button any surface can drop in, and the glyph viewer gains it for kanji. The data now covers every WaniKani kanji as well as the school grades - the characters WaniKani teaches past the joyo list were silently missing, and those are the ones a learner is least sure how to write.

name: Refresh the catalogue export
summary: The script that exports the WaniKani catalogue could not run at all - it imported a server-only module - so its committed snapshot had drifted to 3,930 of 9,324 subjects. Fixed and regenerated, and dropping the raw payload makes the complete export smaller than the stale one was.

name: Official readings on every surface
summary: The grade explorer was not the only place showing readings a character never takes on its own: 245 of the 2,211 JLPT kanji carried them too, so the JLPT explorer, the glyph viewer and search all did. One shared helper now prefers the joyo table wherever readings leave the database.

name: Say what the readings actually are
summary: The grade page claimed its readings were the ones approved for that school year. They are the joyo table's, which is the official list for general use and is not split by year, so the copy now says so.

name: Stroke order from search
summary: A kanji in the search results opens its stroke order without leaving the page. Radicals and vocabulary do not offer it, since neither is a single character with a stroke sequence.

name: Printable writing practice
summary: A printable tracing sheet for any school grade: each character once at full weight to copy, faint repeats to trace, then empty squares to write unaided, with the guide lines a Japanese workbook uses. Drawn from the real stroke paths rather than a greyed-out font.

name: Practice sheets for any list
summary: Writing practice is no longer only for school grades: the same sheet prints a WaniKani level or a JLPT level, so the ladder you are actually climbing is the one you can practise writing.

name: Practice reachable from the nav
summary: Writing practice joins the Explore group instead of hiding behind the grades page, and the sheet keeps the site header on screen while dropping it for print. A nested page no longer lights up its parent's tab as well as its own.

name: An account has its own address
summary: Every account gets a permanent slug and a display name it can change. Pages resolve by either the slug or the old WaniKani username, so links already shared keep working, and an account with no WaniKani connection is now reachable at all.

name: The study queue menu fits on a phone again
summary: The Reviews menu was anchored to its right edge to keep it on screen on a desktop, which pushed it off the left edge on a phone, where the panel is nearly as wide as the display. It now anchors left on small screens and flips right only where there is room.

name: Layout checks at phone, tablet and desktop
summary: Every page is now loaded at three widths and checked for anything hanging outside the screen, with the study menus opened and checked the same way. Its first run found the library upload card running off the side of a phone, which is now fixed.

name: A profile page for every member
summary: Settings now opens on a profile: change the name other members see, record a JLPT certificate, and read a table of every game you have finished. WaniKani level stays read-only because WaniKani sets it, and an account with no WaniKani connection reads Not connected instead of showing a blank.

name: Members without WaniKani can reach their own pages
summary: Page access matched on a WaniKani username, so an account that signed in with Google and never connected WaniKani was turned away from every page it owns - its own profile included - while its API calls kept working. Access now matches the permanent slug first and falls back to the username, so links shared earlier still resolve.

name: The sign-in screen stops offering a door that goes nowhere
summary: Back to leaderboard is hidden for viewers the home page would send straight back, so the button no longer returns you to the page you are already reading. The screen also sends a member who has an account but no WaniKani connection to their own page instead of bouncing them through the invite form.

name: Signing in and out follows one path
summary: Asking for the login page while already signed in answered with a sign-out screen. It now takes you where you were headed, or to your own page. The sign-out tab links straight to the one screen that signs you out instead of bouncing through a redirect with no page of its own, and calls it Sign out, the wording used everywhere else.

name: Signing up, and choosing who can see you
summary: A newcomer now gets a welcome instead of a locked door: what UmaKuma is, that WaniKani is not required, a name, and a choice of who can see them, which they can change on their profile whenever they like. Leaderboards respect that choice. Who may join, what they start on and which questions are asked are all set from a new admin page, and it ships closed.

name: One menu that knows what the header knows
summary: The account menu kept its own copy of the navigation beside the header's, and the two had drifted apart. It now reads the same sections the header does, so nothing can go missing again. On a desktop it drops the navigation entirely, since the header already shows it, and keeps only your account, settings, admin and preferences. Settings moves out of the header into the menu, and Updates is reachable without hunting for the version number in the footer.

name: Rows for the grade explorer, and quieter cards
summary: The grade explorer can be read as rows as well as cards, which is how you scan a whole school year and the only way to see a kanji with ten kun readings in full. The stroke control no longer sits on every card: it appears when you hover, or always where there is no hover to give, which also fixes it covering the end of a long reading.

name: Existing members stay on the public leaderboard
summary: Accounts that predate the visibility setting now read as public, which is what they already were. Reading them as members-only had emptied the leaderboard for anyone who was not signed in. New accounts still start private, where no audience is being taken away.

name: The welcome page accepts an invite session
summary: An invited member may have no Google account at all, and the welcome page assumed one - sending them to the sign-in screen from a page they were entitled to open. It now accepts either kind of session and routes them to their own page.

name: Any kanji, in detail, at its own address
summary: The stroke-order panel is now a shared component any surface can open, and every kanji has a public page you can send to someone. Selecting a card in the grade explorer opens it, which is how every other subject grid already behaved. The header carries the readings as well as the meaning, since a reader knows 何 by なに before they know it by what, with the stroke count beside it and the credit centred at the foot.

name: Updates leads with the release name
summary: Each release now shows its codename on the row rather than only inside it, since that is the part anyone remembers. Months collapse, and an admin reaches the release admin page from here instead of finding their own way.

name: A stroke-order sheet, and honesty about phones
summary: Writing practice can now be printed as a stroke-order chart: one numbered square per stroke, the character built up to that point with the newest stroke picked out. A character of more than eight strokes runs onto a second row instead of shrinking the squares. On a phone the sheet now says plainly that it wants a bigger screen, rather than rendering squares too small to write inside.

name: The practice sheet keeps the sheet you chose
summary: Changing grade or turning the page dropped you back to the tracing sheet, because only the sheet toggle carried the choice. Every link on the page keeps it now.

name: The stroke sheet reads like a practice book
summary: Every row is a full eight squares now: the finished character faintly at the start to work from, the strokes after it, and empty squares filling out the rest of the line. Each row is also titled with the character itself before its meaning.

name: Change the sheet without leaving it
summary: Selecting the source you are already on opens a second row holding every value it offers: the eight school grades, sixty WaniKani levels or five JLPT levels. Changing sheet meant going back to the grade page and in again, which made a page you might print several of from harder to use than it needed to be.

name: Rows on every explorer, and headers that line up
summary: The WaniKani and JLPT explorers can be read as rows as well as cards, which the grade explorer already offered and they did not. The four pages behind the Explore tabs also shared no wrapper, so the sub-nav sat at three different heights and moving between tabs nudged the whole header; they now agree exactly.

name: The practice sheet asks instead of assuming
summary: Whether the finished character sits in the first column is now a checkbox rather than a decision made for you, and the readings can print beside each meaning. The chooser also closes when you pick what is already picked, or with a Done button at the end of the row.

name: Print a sheet from your own lists
summary: Trouble and Favourites are now sources for a writing sheet, offered from the practice page itself rather than only where the tags were made. They stay quiet until the control row is hovered, and appear always on a touch screen where there is no hover to give.

name: Grades reads like its sibling explorers
summary: Filters and results shared one card on the grade explorer, divided by a hairline, while both other explorers keep them in separate cards. They are separate here too now, and the result count sits with the results rather than with the filters.

name: Turning off the finished character clears its square
summary: The option reached the stroke-order sheet but not the tracing sheet, which kept printing the character solid in the first square - the one thing the option exists to remove. It is now an empty square to write in, like the rest of the row.

name: The JLPT as it was before 2010
summary: The explorer and the writing sheet both offer the four levels the test ran until 2009, for anyone who sat it then. Both schemes count down, so old Level 4 is the beginner paper and matches N5 rather than N4 - and N3 is absent, because it was added in 2010 to bridge old Levels 3 and 2. The explorer says so rather than inventing a mapping.

name: Map mode reaches the United States and Canada
summary: Fifty-one states and thirteen provinces and territories join the forty-seven prefectures, as a bonus over the same board rather than a second game. Japan stays the default everywhere, and nothing new is stored: each question's target already carries its country in its id range, so runs recorded before this still read as Japan.

name: Choose the country you play the map on
summary: Map mode's setup now offers Japan, the United States or Canada, and the item count follows the choice - forty-seven, fifty-one or thirteen. Only Map shows the control, because only Map plays somewhere. Adding Europe or Asia later is a dataset and a line in one list, not a new game.

name: The map board follows the question
summary: A Canadian round drew the Japanese coastline: the question knew its country and the board did not. The board now reads the country off the question, and the lobby offers only countries whose maps are real - the American and Canadian outlines are placeholder shapes, so they wait until that is fixed rather than being offered unplayable.

name: Real maps for the United States and Canada
summary: Map mode plays on all three countries. The American and Canadian outlines were hand-drawn placeholders - Ontario was five points - and are now built from the Census Bureau and Natural Earth by scripts that can be re-run when a boundary changes. Neighbours come from the map itself, so the wrong answers are the places next door.

name: Counts where you choose, preferences where your account is
summary: The writing sheet's second row of chips now carries counts, so picking a grade or level is no longer a choice between bare numbers. Theme and Japanese font move from the account menu onto the profile, which already held the name and the visibility - one home for how you want UmaKuma to be rather than two.

name: Every choice visible, and one rule for page width
summary: Two small regions close together put their handles in the same few pixels, so a choice could be hidden behind another and never clicked - Prince Edward Island behind Nova Scotia. A handle now hangs below its region when the space above is taken. Scoreboards say which country a map run was played on, and member pages follow one width rule instead of three.

name: Name the capital, find the region
summary: Map mode can ask by capital city: the prompt names the seat of government and the answer is the region that governs from it. Bismarck is North Dakota, Victoria is British Columbia. It works on all three countries, because every dataset already recorded a capital for every region.

name: Capitals that actually ask something
summary: The capitals round now skips the twenty-nine Japanese prefectures that share their capital's name, so it asks the eighteen worth knowing: 札幌市 is Hokkaido, 横浜市 is Kanagawa, 名古屋市 is Aichi. Japanese capitals are written in kanji now too, matching the tiles rather than sitting in romaji in a Japanese round.

name: Pagers where the page needs them
summary: Paging is a shared component now, and where it sits is the surface's choice: top, bottom, both or none. The writing practice sheet takes both, because its only Next link used to be three thousand pixels below the fold, past three sheets of empty tracing squares.

name: A sheet that prints like a worksheet
summary: Printing a writing sheet now gives you a worksheet: Letter with proper margins, a Name and Date rule at the top, characters that never split across a page break, and none of the site's footer or version banner. The faint tracing characters print faintly instead of vanishing into the browser's ink saving.

name: Squares sized for who is writing
summary: The writing sheet offers three square sizes. Large gives a child six big boxes to form characters in; Small gives an adult ten smaller ones and an extra tracing repetition, which is what copying at volume actually wants. Medium is the practice-book square the sheet always had.

name: Prints on the paper you have
summary: The sheet named Letter as its paper size, which overrode the printer: an A4 tray produced a Letter page scaled down inside it. It now pins only the orientation and lets the paper be whatever is loaded, so A4 and 8.5x11 both come out filling the page.

name: Choose these
summary: Choosing items is a surface control now, sitting beside the grid and list toggle rather than being a feature of the practice page. Pick characters on the grades explorer and send them to a sheet; the chosen set travels in the link, so a sheet built by hand is shareable and printable before anything is saved. Destinations are offered to a chosen set rather than built into the picking.

name: Saved lists
summary: Choose characters on the grades explorer, give the set a name, and it keeps: Week 1, Week 2. A Lists page shows every set you have built with the characters it holds rather than a count, and each one goes straight to a practice sheet. The same idea as Trouble and Favourites, with a name instead of a flag.

name: JLPT kanji without WaniKani
summary: JLPT kanji are readable by any signed-in member now, connected to WaniKani or not. The table never had a WaniKani column; the query just happened to live inside an admin route, and the member-facing path went through an endpoint that decrypts a WaniKani token. The query is shared now and serves the readings themselves rather than the admin view's counts of them.

name: Admin that works on a phone
summary: The accounts list becomes labelled cards below tablet width, so level, due count, sync state and invite code stop hiding behind a sideways scroll on a 980px table. The pagination row wraps instead of pushing every admin panel wider than the screen, the tab strip fades at its cut edge rather than slicing a pill mid-word, and the Data tab asks its two questions as two short rows instead of four wrapping pills.

name: Grades and Maps in Data
summary: The Data tab covers school grades and map regions, not just WaniKani and JLPT. Both ship as files in the repo and reach the app through scripts somebody has to remember to run, so the panels answer the question those scripts leave open: does what shipped match what is loaded. Grades compares every grade file against the database row count; Maps shows each country's region count, geometry detail, regions with no shared border, and where the data came from.

name: Print the whole sheet
summary: Print asks how much: this page, or everything. It printed the twenty characters on screen and nothing else, so a grade of eighty was four separate print jobs - and because twenty characters is about two and a half sheets of paper, three of those four ended in a mostly-empty page. Everything drops the reading pages and lets the characters flow, which takes grade three from ten jobs and thirty sheets to one job and twenty-six. Lists too long for one document split into print runs rather than rendering 1,110 characters at once. Where the pager sits is no longer a question the sheet asks.

name: Pages that are sheets of paper
summary: A screen page is three sheets of paper now, so printing one comes out whole. It was twenty characters at every square size - a number about the screen, not about paper - and twenty medium squares is two and a half sheets, so the third sheet of every page came out 40% blank. The counts were measured by adding characters one at a time and watching where the paper broke: seventeen large, twenty-two medium, twenty-six small, each landing on a US Letter sheet boundary and taking the same three sheets on A4. Rows are numbered as well, by their place in the whole list rather than the page, so page two runs 23 to 44 and a sheet can be set as numbers twelve to twenty.

name: Map handles that read in order
summary: Map handles are numbered west to east, so a round reads 1 2 3 4 across the map instead of the 3 2 4 1 the shuffle happened to deal - and pressing 1 now means the leftmost handle. They also stop overlapping: the old rule called two handles clear at 1.9 radii when circles of radius r touch at 2, so every pair it passed was already into its neighbour, and it had only two positions to try, which left a third crowded region back on top of the first. Handles now try a column of positions and take the first that is clear, vertical before sideways so the numbering survives. Across 48,000 handles on all three maps: no overlaps and none cropped at the frame.

name: Japanese that survives translation
summary: Chrome's translate offer used to eat the site. On the grades explorer it replaced every kanji with its English meaning - 一 became "one", 右 became "right" - beside a card already printing that same meaning underneath, and it romanised the readings, so a page teaching kanji showed no kanji at all. Every Japanese element now carries both refusals, the HTML5 translate attribute and Google's notranslate class, while the English chrome around it stays translatable for anyone who needs it. The font class and the glyph sizing helper each carry the marker with them, since anything drawn in the Japanese face is Japanese, and a unit test keeps the raw font class out of the rest of the tree so the next glyph surface cannot take the styling and forget the protection. Release notes that quote Japanese inside an English sentence mark only the quote. Audited across sixteen pages: no unprotected Japanese left.

name: The rest of the translation ward
summary: The previous release protected what a page draws on arrival and nothing else, so the stroke-order modal still showed "circle" where 円 belonged in both its Gothic and Mincho previews, and the shared explorer card lost its protection the moment a list switched to rows. Those and the game's match prompt are covered now, along with the admin kanji tables. A second half to it: translation was also respacing compact chips, because a label built from several JSX children is several text nodes with the gaps between them up for grabs - "JLPT N5" came back as "JLPTN5", "APPR - SRS 4" as "APPR- SRS4", and every count as "( 157 )". Codes and counts are now single strings that refuse translation, while prose like "Showing 1-60 of 80 kanji" still reads in whatever language the reader wants. A source guard fails the build on any element that reaches for a Japanese typeface without refusing translation, which is what would have caught the modal.

name: Japanese declared as Japanese
summary: Two releases of marking Japanese element by element kept missing places, because the cause was never addressed: the kanji were not declared as Japanese, so a browser counted them, decided the whole page was Japanese, and offered to translate it into English - pushing the English through a Japanese-to-English model on the way, which is how "Writing practice" came back as "First practice" and "Shellfish" as "shellfish". Every Japanese run now carries lang="ja" beside its refusal, which is what the spec asks for: an English document with declared exceptions. That leaves the interface translatable for somebody who needs it in another language, where a blanket refusal at the root would have taken that away, and it tells a screen reader to read a reading with Japanese pronunciation rather than spelling the kanji out as English.

name: Translation refused at the root
summary: The previous release bet that declaring every Japanese run lang="ja" would stop Chrome reading the page as Japanese and offering to translate it into English. It did not: "always translate Japanese" is a sticky preference, and once it is set the page's own declarations do not get a vote. So the page refuses translation at the root again. What Chrome was doing is running every string through a Japanese-to-English model, English included, which re-interprets rather than passes through - "Writing practice" came back "First practice". The lang="ja" tagging stays because it is correct and because a screen reader needs it to pronounce a reading instead of spelling the kanji out as English. The cost is that Google Translate can no longer render the interface in another language; the answer to that is a locale layer serving translations we wrote, which the copy modules are already shaped for.

name: The board stops leaking
summary: /api/leaderboard took no session and applied no filter: it selected from Account directly and handed every member's nickname and real WaniKani username to anyone who asked, children included, while the home page had long since moved to the filtered loader. The route was serving nobody in the app and leaking to everybody. It now requires a session and reuses loadLeaderboardAccounts, so one place decides who may be seen - each member's own visibility choice plus the admin's approval - and a signed-in stranger with no account here sees what a stranger sees. The background sync trigger moved behind the same check; it was reachable anonymously, which let anyone on the internet make the server start refreshing accounts against the WaniKani API.

name: A header with room in it
summary: Search was a 96px box that grew to 160px on focus, because three things were competing for the right-hand end of one row: the field, the release codename, and a menu button floating past both. The codename moves to the second row, which every section already drew, and search takes the space it left - 224px rising to 320px on a wide screen - sitting directly beside the menu rather than across the row from it. The second row is now always present, so the header is the same height on every page and the content below stops jumping as you navigate. On a phone search collapses to its icon and opens a full-width field under the header, the way WaniKani and most narrow headers do it; an always-present field there cost about 150px and silently pushed Admin off the end of a row that clips rather than wraps.

name: The third door, closed
summary: /api/join created accounts and never asked whether signing up was allowed. It took a Google session and a WaniKani token and upserted an account straight into the database - no invite code, no signup mode, no approval - so the whole invite-only model could be walked around by anyone who could sign in with Google and hold any working WaniKani token. It had no caller anywhere in the app, having been replaced by the invite panel, and it is deleted rather than gated: a gate would have reopened it the moment open signup was switched on, and it would then have created accounts that skipped the onboarding wizard and the approval queue as well.

name: Admin joins the header
summary: Admin was the last place still drawing its own navigation strip - a centred segmented control in a third row below the header, while every other section put its pages on the left of the header's second row. Its tabs move into that same slot and read the same way, so an admin page and a study page are recognisably the same site. The header's second row now accepts a section that supplies its own pages, which admin needs since its tabs come from their own registry rather than from navSections. They are links rather than buttons as well, restoring middle-click and open-in-new-tab that the router.push control had eaten. Three roadmap entries were also removed from the planned list: they described work already shipped under other names, so the page was advertising as planned things that were live.

name: Search that answers while you type
summary: The header search box waited for Enter and a full page load before showing anything, which is a long way round for a learner who just wants to know where a kanji lives. Now the ten best hits appear under the field as you type, one row per glyph with its meaning, reading and source, ranked by the same scoring the results page uses. The dropdown reuses the existing search endpoint, whose per-query CDN caching means most keystrokes are answered at the edge without touching the database - prefixes are shared by everyone typing them. Arrow keys walk the rows and Enter opens the highlighted hit straight in your own explorer, falls through to the see-all footer, or submits the full search as before; a signed-out visitor gets the results page instead of links that would bounce off the sign-in wall. Japanese suggests from the first character, since one kanji is a real question, while Latin waits for two, since one letter matches half the catalogue.

name: A menu that lists everything
summary: The account menu offered two admin links, "Admin" and "Manage users", while admin had nine pages - so seven of them existed only for somebody who already knew the header was there. It reads the same registry the admin header reads now, so adding an admin page adds it to the menu. The menu also stops shouting: each cluster used to be a bordered card under an uppercase heading, ACCOUNT and GO TO and SETTINGS and ADMIN and ACTIONS, so a dozen links read as five boxed lists. It is one flat column with a hairline where the subject changes, and it hangs off the button it belongs to rather than being pinned to a corner of the window, which is what made it read as floating loose of the header. Game gets its second row as well: six games that were reachable only by scrolling to the hub cards now sit in the header beside every other section's pages.

name: Search understands romaji
summary: The search placeholder promised "or romaji" and the code never kept the promise: readings are stored in kana, so typing watashi found nothing while わたし found plenty. A query is now folded into every spelling it could mean - the raw text, its hiragana, and its katakana, since JLPT stores on'yomi in katakana - and all three catalogues match and rank against the full set, scoring each hit by its best variant so folding can never demote a result the raw text already earned. The fold is a plain syllable table that accepts Hepburn and common kunrei spellings, doubled consonants, and the n-before-consonant rule, and it refuses to convert anything that is not entirely romaji, so English words never gain a phantom kana reading that outranks their real meaning match.

name: One search box, everywhere
summary: The header box and the search page's box were two different controls, and the page you were sent to was the one without autocomplete. Both now run the same combobox: suggestions while you type, the rest of the best match drawn in faint grey after the caret with Enter locking it in as if typed, a clear button once there is something to clear, and the magnifier itself as the submit. Arrowing through the suggestions rewrites the box without spending a single extra search, because what was typed and what is displayed are kept apart - the request still keys on the typed text while the box shows the highlighted row. At rest the header field is half its working width and grows when it is wanted, the results page keeps the site navigation instead of dropping it, and the arrow keys carry on past the last suggestion into the results themselves and back up into the box.

name: A rejection that means something
summary: Turning an account down used to do almost nothing. A rejected member kept their session, opened their own pages, and answered every study, tag and game route as before - the only thing rejection changed was that they stopped appearing on the leaderboard, which is to say the admin's one sanction was to make somebody invisible to everyone except themselves. It now closes four doors at once: the owner check every /api/study and /api/custom-study route runs through, the viewer resolution that the user pages and the header are built on, the invite cookie (cleared on the next request rather than at some later sign-in), and signup, which will not hand back an account it has turned away or let the same email make a second one. A rejected member lands on a plain notice instead, with no reason given and no appeal form - a reason tells somebody acting in bad faith what to change, and a form hands them a channel. Being turned away stays separate from being merely pending: somebody still waiting keeps the run of the site, which is what the signup copy promises them, so the lock is written as "rejected" rather than "not approved". Accounts predating the column read as approved, because a lock that defaulted the other way would shut out the whole family on deploy.

name: Colour on screen, ink on paper
summary: The writing practice page was built as a print preview and painted like one: white background, neutral greys, black text, from the source chips at the top to the squares at the bottom. It was the one page in the app that looked like a photocopy of the rest of it. Everything on screen now uses the site's own palette - the chips take the accent, the sheet sits on a surface card the way every other list does, the guide squares are drawn in the line colour and the tracing strokes in a pale accent, which is what a Japanese workbook prints them in anyway. None of it reaches paper: every colour on a printed element states its printed grey beside itself, the sheet's card drops its border and padding so the squares start at the printer's margin, and a rule under the whole region strips any background a later panel might bring with it. A test reads the sheet's own source and fails on a colour that says nothing about how it prints.

name: Readings that stay in the box
summary: In the grade explorer's list view, a kanji with many kun readings ran its readings straight out through the right-hand edge of its row. 下 has eight of them and they crossed the card border, the JLPT pill and whatever sat beside it. The text had been asked to truncate, but a flex item's floor is the width of its own content, so the paragraph holding the readings simply sat as wide as they measured and the truncation inside it never had a narrower box to work against. Measured after the fix at 393, 650 and 1440 pixels: no row overflows its card by a single pixel, and the page has no horizontal scroll.

name: A door for crawlers
summary: There was no robots.txt at all, so every crawler that found the site walked all of it - including each member's pages, which are built per request from that member's own data and render a refusal to anybody who is not them. The writing practice sheets made it acute: source, level, sheet size, mode and page all ride in the URL, which is what makes a sheet shareable and also means one school grade is thousands of distinct addresses to a bot following links. That one route took 3,200 serverless invocations in twelve hours, on a site with eight accounts, and the project's daily CPU went from about two minutes to nine and a half the week practice shipped. Member pages, admin, the API and the search results page are now closed; the home page, the release notes, the news pages and the per-character kanji pages stay open, because a family site nobody can find is not more private for it. The rules are tested against the route tree rather than a second copy of the list, so a member page added later is either covered or fails the build.

name: Shift-click takes the row
summary: Choosing characters was one click per character, so picking a row of five in the grade explorer took five clicks and picking forty took forty. Shift-click now takes everything between the last card and this one, the way it works in a file browser or a mail client, in either direction and from either end. The range only ever adds - a sweep that unpicked half of what it crossed would be impossible to predict from where it began - and the far end becomes the new anchor, so a selection can be walked outward a stretch at a time. A keyboard user gets it without a second set of handlers: activating a card with Enter or Space reports the modifiers held at the time, so Shift and Enter sweeps the same range. The logic sits in the shared selection hook rather than in the grade grid, so the next surface to offer choosing inherits it, and the hint appears in the selection bar only once something is picked, which is the first moment a range is possible.

name: Search pages its results
summary: Search asked for every match at once and rendered all of it: the query "a" is 122 rows across the three catalogues, and the dropdown threw away all but ten of them after the request had already been paid for. Both surfaces now take a window. The API accepts a limit and an offset, sliced after ranking so the totals and the per-source counts still describe the whole answer; the dropdown starts at ten rows and grows a stretch at a time as the highlight or the scroll comes within reach of the end, up to forty, past which the answer is the results page; and the results page renders its first twenty, appending the next twenty as the reader nears the bottom or presses the button under the list. The dropdown widens its window from zero rather than stepping by offset, because it keeps one row per glyph and a duplicate can straddle any boundary, so a superset is the only window that cannot reorder rows under the highlight.

name: An empty search box opens search
summary: Clicking the magnifier with nothing typed did nothing at all: the submit refused an empty query, so the only way to reach the search page from the header was to type something and then delete it once you arrived. Enter on an empty box was the same dead end. Empty now means take me to search, which is what pressing a search button with nothing to search plainly asks for, and the rule lives in one shared helper so the header, the phone sheet and the search page's own box all answer the same way.

name: The way out of the dropdown
summary: The see all results row sat at the bottom left of the suggestion list in the same small type as a result, so the one control that leaves the dropdown read as an eleventh, oddly worded result. It is now centred across the full width, set in the same uppercase weight the rest of the site gives an action, and separated from the rows above by its own rule, with the highlighted state tinted rather than greyed so arrowing onto it looks like landing on a button rather than on another row.

name: The searches you already ran
summary: Looking a kanji up is rarely a single act - you check 家, then 家事, then go back to 家 - and retyping it each time was the whole friction. The search page now keeps the searches this browser has run and lists five of them under the results, each one a link back to those results and each with its own way to forget it. Twenty are remembered while five are shown, so forgetting one reveals the sixth rather than leaving a gap, and a single control clears the lot. The history lives on the device rather than the account, which means an anonymous visitor gets the same convenience as a member, and it is read through a store subscription rather than into state after mount, so the panel never flashes empty before it fills.

name: Rows that show the character
summary: The JLPT and WaniKani explorers share one card component, and its list view was unusable: where each row s character should have been there was a pile of chips instead - the level pill sitting on the success rate sitting on the glyph. Both explorers hand the card an overlay written for the card shape, which places the level, the success rate and the trouble and favourite controls in the corners of a glyph box 128 pixels tall. A row s glyph box is 44 pixels square and has no corners to spare, so everything landed on top of everything else. The card now tells its overlays which shape they are being drawn into: in a row they lay themselves out in the line as ordinary chips and buttons, while the card keeps the corners it was designed around. Neither explorer changed - they pass the same overlay as before - and the trouble and favourite controls now work from the list view as well as the grid, which is what a member scanning a long level actually wants. Measured on both explorers afterwards: forty row glyph boxes each, none holding anything but the character.

name: The link goes where it says
summary: Clicking WaniKani in the header while on the JLPT explorer changed the address and nothing else - the JLPT explorer stayed on screen under a URL that said library-explorer. Each explorer has its own path but they all rewrite to the one user page with a dashboard parameter, so moving between them re-renders the tab component instead of remounting it, and the active tab was seeded from its prop by useState, which reads its argument once and ignores every later value. The tab now follows the address it is given, adjusted during render rather than in an effect so the old tab is never painted first and corrected a frame later. The bare user page is deliberately left out: that address names no tab, and following the prop there would overwrite the member s last open tab on every visit.

name: The strokes button stops floating
summary: In the grade explorer s list view the stroke-order button was positioned absolutely at the right-hand edge of each row and revealed on hover, so it came down on top of the JLPT pill it was meant to sit beside. The row had reserved padding for it, but the pills spread into that space anyway and the two ended up in the same place - reserving room was never going to be the fix, because a row s controls have to take part in the layout. It sits in the line now, as the last thing in the row s chip cluster, taking its own room rather than floating over whatever is underneath. The card view is unchanged: there the button has a free corner to occupy, and one permanent control on every card of a screenful is noise rather than help, so it stays where it was and still waits for hover.

name: Study opens from anywhere
summary: Tapping Study in the header sometimes did nothing - the address changed and whatever explorer was open stayed on screen. It was only sometimes because from the study page itself the link looked fine, and it was worst on a phone, where the header is the only navigation there is. The cause sat one level below the tab that was fixed in 0.164.0: /study rewrites to dashboard=learn and the bare user page carries no parameter at all, and both resolve to the same tab, so the page could not tell go to study from landed here. The bare page has to reopen whichever tab the member last had, and that restore was overwriting an explicit request to open Study. The two are now told apart at the point the address is read, so a named tab always wins and an unnamed one still restores. The /study rewrite also matched nothing in the resolver and only worked by falling through to the default; it is handled explicitly now.

name: Every section on a phone
summary: A phone header showed four sections - Leaderboard, Study, Game, Admin - chosen by a hardcoded list of labels. Explore, Progress and Read were not in the markup at all, so on a phone the explorers, the progress pages and the reading pages could only be reached by somebody who already knew the menu button held them. Seven labels will not fit 393 pixels, so the row scrolls sideways now, reusing the same treatment the admin tab row has had for a while: no visible scrollbar, and a fade at the right edge that says there is more, which lifts once you reach the end. Removing the allowlist also removes seven literal labels that would have quietly stopped matching the day a section was renamed.

name: Choose a range anywhere
summary: Choosing a set of characters existed in the grade explorer and nowhere else, and the JLPT explorer had no way to select anything at all - so building a practice sheet or a saved list from a JLPT level meant picking the kanji out by hand somewhere else. The JLPT explorer now offers the same Choose mode, the same bar, and the same two destinations, and shift-click takes everything between the last card and this one. None of that is a second copy: the bar and its destinations moved into a shared component that the grade board now uses too, and the card draws the ring and the tick itself so a chosen card reads the same on every surface. The tick sits where the index number was, because every corner of the card is already spoken for by a pill, a level, a success rate or the trouble and favourite controls, and a tick laid over any of them hides something the member is using to choose. The WaniKani explorer keeps its own selection - it picks subject ids and carries bulk operations the others have no use for - but it no longer carries its own copy of the range maths, and that fixed a bug in passing: its anchor was the item position in the visible list, so changing a filter or loading another page moved every position underneath it and the next shift-click swept the wrong stretch. It anchors on the subject now, which survives both.

name: Choose a range on every list
summary: Choosing reached the explorers in 0.168.0 and stopped there, which left the two surfaces where a member has already gathered something deliberately - their study history, and the Trouble and Favourites lists - with no way to act on a set. Scanning what you got wrong last week is exactly the position from which you want those characters on a practice sheet, and the only route was to write them down. Both now offer the same Choose mode, in both densities, with shift taking everything between the last pick and this one. The work went into the shared row and card pair rather than into either surface, so neither had to learn anything: they pass the selection through and get the tick, the highlight and the sweep for free, and the next list built on that pair inherits all of it. The tick sits before history is own correct or wrong mark rather than replacing it, because whether you got it right is exactly what you are reading when you decide whether to pick that one. Where a surface cannot know which member it belongs to - the tagged lists open from the game lobby, from history, from either explorer - the practice offer is withheld rather than pointed at a guess.

name: One sweep, one anchor
summary: The study explorer had shift-click already, and had it wrong in the same way the WaniKani explorer did: the anchor a range was measured from was the item is position in the filtered list, which stops meaning anything the moment a filter changes or another page loads. Change a status chip after picking one item and the next shift-click swept a stretch the member never crossed. It anchors on the subject now, which survives both, and it uses the same range helper the other four surfaces use rather than a third copy of the arithmetic. That is all of them: the three explorers, study history and the tagged lists now sweep a range the same way, and a test names each surface so a sixth cannot quietly go without.

name: Your two lists, on your lists page
summary: Trouble and Favourites are lists in every sense a member cares about - they are named, they hold subjects, they are what you practise from - but they are tag rows rather than saved lists, so the page whose whole job is showing a member their lists was the one place they never appeared. They could be reached only through a panel opened by a button somewhere else, which meant the two lists a member had actually built were the two they could not find. Both now sit at the top of the lists page, in the same card as every saved list, with a count and a preview of what is in them. What differs is what they cannot do: there is nothing to delete, because untagging the last item empties a list rather than removing it, so the card offers Open instead and the panel is where tagging still happens. Their practice sheet is addressed by source rather than by the characters on the card, so printing one takes the whole list instead of the two dozen the card had room to preview. Both are always shown, empty ones included, because no favourites yet is an answer to the question somebody came to this page with and a missing card is not. The subtitle stopped claiming every list here was built by hand, which two of them now are not.

name: Recent searches join the list
summary: The remembered searches shipped as a card of their own below the results, which read as a separate widget parked under the page rather than as part of what the reader was already scanning. They are now the last rows of the results list itself: the same card, the same row rhythm, the same lane the glyphs occupy - a history icon standing where a glyph would - introduced by a tinted band carrying the heading and the control that clears them, because a search you already ran is a way back rather than an answer and has to be told apart from the results above it at a glance. The end of the results moved inside the list too, so what closes the results sits with them instead of floating below the card. With no list to close out - no query yet, or a query that matched nothing - the rows carry the same card on their own.

name: Permanent lists, kept apart
summary: Trouble and Favourites arrived on the lists page in the last release and sat in the same grid as the saved lists, which quietly misrepresented both. They are permanent - they fill themselves as a member tags while studying, and there is nothing to delete because untagging the last item empties a list rather than removing it - while a saved list is made and thrown away at will. Run together, the grid invited a member to look for a delete on a card that does not have one. Each kind now has its own section under a heading that says what it is: Always here, which cannot be deleted, and Saved by you, which can. The card markup was extracted rather than duplicated per section, so both kinds still render through one component. The saved section says only what the page can actually do today - renaming a list is not built yet, and the copy does not pretend otherwise.

name: Let the database sleep
summary: The study counts and the study queue each re-asked the server every thirty seconds, which is far more often than either can change: review counts move on WaniKani SRS schedule, measured in hours, and the queue is mutated locally as a member answers rather than discovered by polling. The poll was never the mechanism, only a safety net for a session left open while something changed elsewhere - and it was an expensive one. A single open tab was 120 serverless invocations an hour and roughly 240 database queries, since every request checks access and then reads the account again; an evening across the family ran to thousands of both while discovering nothing. The part that actually shows up on the bill is Neon: its compute suspends after five minutes idle and is charged for the time it is awake, so a thirty-second poll meant the database never slept for as long as anybody had the study page open. Both surfaces now poll on one shared interval of five minutes, set just past that suspend threshold on purpose, so a closed laptop lets the database go to sleep. Revalidate-on-focus stays on, so returning to the tab still refreshes at once and the slower poll is never something a member waits on. A test pins the interval against the suspend window and fails if either surface goes back to a hand-typed number.

name: One read where there were two
summary: Every study route checked whether the request was allowed by reading the account, then read the same row again for the member WaniKani token. Counts and queue are what the study page asks for on a timer and review is asked once per answer, so that second read was the single most repeated query in the product - and on the busiest paths it doubled the database work for no information. The columns an access decision needs are three small ones, so they are now selected as part of the read the route was making anyway and the round trip disappears. Five routes moved across: counts, queue, review, upcoming and lesson start. The access check itself got cheaper too: it used to query once for the invite path and again for the Google path when the first did not match, and now resolves who is asking from the request before touching the database at all, so an admin is answered without a query and everybody else costs exactly one. Permission and existence stay separate answers, because a permitted request for an account that has since been deleted is a 404 rather than a 401.

name: Two doors that were never locked
summary: Two per-account endpoints had no authentication of any kind. Both take an account id straight from the path, and both read that member encrypted WaniKani token: the JLPT route decrypts it and calls WaniKani with it, and the levels route reads a progress snapshot and writes a fresh one back. Verified against a running server with no cookies at all, a stranger holding an id received that member own kanji progress - subject ids, characters, meanings - and their level snapshot showing what they had learned. Both now answer 401 before touching the database. This was also an uncapped cost vector, which is how it was found: four database queries and an outbound WaniKani call per request, repeatable as fast as anyone cared to ask, on endpoints nothing was rate limiting. The explorers that call them only ever ask about the member whose page they are on, so requiring a session costs nothing that was working. Checked before the row is read rather than after, so a refused request costs one query rather than five.

name: Search reads every meaning
summary: All three catalogues searched every meaning a subject carries and then ranked the hit on its first one alone, so anything matched on another meaning scored zero and was removed by the filter that drops non-matches: the search found the row and then threw it away. Searching magnate returned nothing at all, though it is one of 王's meanings, and home returned twenty-one results while missing 家. Ranking now takes the best score across every meaning the subject holds - including the Heisig keyword, which was searched but never scored - and the row shows the meaning that earned the match behind the one the subject leads with, so a result for magnate no longer reads only King. Against the live catalogues magnate goes from zero hits to two and home from twenty-one to forty-five, while sun still puts 日 first.

name: Closed unless it says otherwise
summary: An API route here was public unless somebody remembered to guard it, and two never did - which is how a stranger came to be able to read a member WaniKani progress by holding an account id. That is the wrong way round for a site whose whole content is members data, so being open is now a decision that has to be written down. A test walks every route file and requires each one to either check who is asking or appear in a list of public routes with the reason it is safe to leave open. A new route that forgets fails the build rather than production, and adding one to that list is a deliberate act a reviewer sees in the diff. The same test checks two other things the list can drift on: that a route listed as public still exists, and that any public route which touches the database or calls an external API is rate limited. It caught one straight away - the book cover proxy, which does two database reads and up to two lookups against openBD and Google Books per call, with nothing throttling it. Its responses cache hard, but a cache only helps a repeated ISBN and varying one walks straight past it, so it is now limited to 120 requests a minute per address. The cache posture everywhere else was already correct: the static catalogue routes cache publicly at the edge for a day or more, and no route behind a session declares a public cache, so nothing personal can be served from a shared one.

name: A way in without an account
summary: Every search result linked into one of the viewer's own explorer pages, which sit behind the sign-in wall, so a reader with no account got no link at all: rows of dead text on the page most likely to be reached by somebody who has never signed in. A single kanji already has a public page - it is the one a shared kanji link opens - so that is where an anonymous reader now goes, from both the results list and the suggestion dropdown. A word or a radical drawn as an image has no page of its own, so those still fall back to the results rather than to a link that would land nowhere, and a signed-in member is unaffected: their explorers carry their review state and remain the better destination.

name: The day a release actually shipped
summary: An evening of releases claimed to have shipped on the 1st of September while it was still the 31st of August here. UTC rolls over seven hours before Vancouver does, and the release dates were written from UTC while every other date in this app - the Daily Challenge key, the study day - is the Vancouver day. The releases page grew a phantom September sitting above a still-running August, and thirty-two entries across two evenings were affected, some of them stamped hours into the future. All of them are corrected to the day they were really shipped on, respaced so each instant falls inside the day it claims. Two tests now hold the line: no release may claim to have shipped in the future, and each entry date must match the Vancouver day of its own timestamp. Nothing caught this before because a UTC date is a perfectly valid date - it was just the wrong one, and only a reader in the right timezone could see it. The admin releases list also collapses now, the way the public one already did: a hundred and seventy-seven entries each showing a full paragraph is a page nobody can scan, so the line identifies the release and the prose waits until it is asked for.

name: The kanji dictionary
summary: The site knew kanji through three partial catalogues - what WaniKani teaches, the JLPT table, and the school grades - each assembled for its own purpose, so a character arrived with one meaning and a handful of readings, and some never arrived at all: the JLPT table holds neither 鬱 nor 苺. KANJIDIC2 is the reference those are footnotes to, and it now ships with the site: 10,384 characters with every English meaning, every on and kun reading, the readings only names use, stroke counts, grades, frequency ranks and the old JLPT levels. It is generated by pnpm kanji:build in the same spirit as the map and stroke data - regenerate, never hand-edit - and read the way the stroke data is read, one file of a few hundred kilobytes at a time rather than all 3.7MB. The public kanji page is the first surface to use it, so the 7,400 characters outside the school curriculum now open with meanings, readings and stroke counts instead of a drawing and nothing to read, and a shared link previews as the character and its meaning. KANJIDIC2 is CC BY-SA 4.0, so the credit sits on every page that shows the data and the generated files carry the licence, which is what share-alike asks for.

name: Renaming a list you saved
summary: A saved list could be created and deleted and nothing in between, so a typo in "Week 1" could only be fixed by throwing the list away and picking every character again. Lists now rename in place: the name becomes a field on the card, Enter saves it, Escape abandons it, and the characters are never touched. Renaming is its own request rather than a save under a new name, which matters more than it sounds - saving under a name that already exists replaces that list's contents, so a rename expressed that way would quietly empty whichever list already held the name. Choosing a name another list has now says so and keeps what was typed, because colliding with "Week 1" is an ordinary thing to do rather than an error to swallow. Names are tidied the same way whether saved or renamed, so "Week  1" and "Week 1" stay one list instead of becoming two nobody can tell apart. The two built-in lists, Trouble and Favourites, offer neither rename nor delete: they fill themselves as you tag while you study, and untagging the last item empties one rather than removing it. Three controls no longer fit a card at the width the grid gives it, so the row wraps rather than breaking "Practise these" across two lines inside its own button, and the condensed view stopped running off the right edge of a phone.

name: Search reads the dictionary
summary: Shipping KANJIDIC2 gave the kanji page 10,384 characters but left search reading the same three catalogues, so 渕 and 煕 - both inside the 1,500 most frequent characters in Japanese - still returned nothing at all. The dictionary is now a fourth source, and it fills gaps rather than adding a fourth copy of every common character: a query for 水 already answers three times over, so the dictionary answers only where no catalogue does, and asking for the dictionary tab on its own is the exception that shows everything it holds. A tie between a catalogue and the dictionary goes to the catalogue, because alphabetical keys would otherwise push a reference row above the row carrying a member's own review state, and a dictionary hit links to the public kanji page since no explorer holds a character nobody teaches.

name: Results that stay on the screen
summary: A hundred results made the search page many screens tall, so scrolling through them carried the navigation, the search box and the source tabs off the top, left the remembered searches below a kilometre of rows, and ended a short answer in a blank field where the list used to be. The rows now scroll inside the card at a height the screen sets, so everything around them stays put: the box, the tabs and the counts hold their place while the results move under them. The recent searches sit outside that scroll rather than at the end of it - a way back you have to scroll a hundred results to reach is not a way back - and the paging observer watches the card instead of the window, so reaching the end of the rows still loads the next stretch.

name: Sentences that show the kanji at work
summary: Readings and meanings say what a kanji is; a sentence says what it does, and the site's own examples come from WaniKani - shown to WaniKani members, absent everywhere else, including the public page a shared kanji link opens. Tatoeba publishes its corpus weekly as plain exports, which is the supported way to take it and the reason nothing here scrapes anything, and 232,731 Japanese sentences with an English translation are now ingested and indexed by the characters they contain. They arrive easiest first: each was scored at ingest by its length and the cost of its hardest character, so 水 opens with 水をくれ！ rather than with one of the other 1,644 sentences it appears in. Near-repeats that differ only in punctuation are folded together, since Tatoeba holds 水をくれ！ and 水をくれ。 separately and both would otherwise spend a slot saying the same thing. Kana-only sentences are kept though nothing can reach them yet, because they are the ones a kana vocabulary word would need later. The corpus is CC BY 2.0 FR, so the credit sits under every set of examples.

name: The campaign selector that actually switches
summary: Picking the other reading campaign on the Check-ins panel did nothing. The select snapped back to the first campaign before anyone could see it move, so a member with two campaigns could only ever look at one of them. Choosing a campaign did set it, and did start a fetch for the new one - but the panel keeps showing the previous response while the next is in flight, and that stale response still named the campaign being left. A rule that let the server's answer overrule the member's put the selection straight back. The member's choice now wins whenever it names a campaign that exists; the server's answer still seeds the choice on arrival and still rescues it if the campaign it named has been deleted. Found by repairing the smoke suite rather than by anyone reporting it, which is the first thing that suite has caught since it started telling the truth.

name: Text you can actually read
summary: Muted grey text across the app sat at 3.07 to one against a 4.5 floor - readable if your eyes are good and the room is bright, and not otherwise. It was on 751 nodes, and nothing about it looked wrong to whoever chose it, which is how contrast problems survive: faint reads as tasteful to the person picking it and as missing to the person who cannot see it. Every muted step below the readable one is raised to the lowest that clears the floor against both the white surface and the page background. The three subject colours had the same problem as pill labels - the radical pill worst at 2.21, half what a small uppercase label needs - but those colours are the brand, so they are untouched. A second, darker token was added for text on a tinted ground, and only pill labels use it; every glyph, border, fill and accent still reads the original. Faintness is kept where it carries meaning: a disabled pagination button, the off state of a toggle, the greyed corner a round is not using, the ghost completion that must not look typed, and the glyph drawn behind stroke order to trace over. Those are listed one by one with the reason, and a test holds the floor everywhere else.

name: Names the site keeps for itself
summary: A handful of words now cannot become a member's address. Signing up as Admin or Support would have produced /users/admin and /users/support, which read as the site speaking rather than as a member - and the first person to get one would have taken it by accident rather than by malice, since the address is built from whatever display name they arrived with. Reserved words are treated exactly like a name somebody already has: they take the numbered suffix, so nobody is refused an account and only the address moves. Their display name is untouched. Worth saying what this is not: it was written down as a route-shadowing risk and it never was one. Every member page lives under /users/ and there is no dynamic segment at the root, so /admin is the admin page whatever anyone calls themselves. The backlog note has been corrected rather than quietly deleted.

name: Somewhere for a selection to go
summary: Choosing items on the study and WaniKani explorers could only ever be undone. Both run a bulk mode with shift-click ranges, and the panel counted what you had gathered and offered Select Visible, Clear and Done - nothing to actually do with the set. Meanwhile the grade and JLPT explorers, which choose through a different mechanism, had two destinations from the start: save it as a list, print it as a practice sheet. Those destinations belong to the act of choosing rather than to either mechanism, so they now live on the shared bulk panel and both explorers gain them at once. Practice takes only the kanji: a study queue is radicals and vocabulary too, and a practice sheet is squares to write kanji in - the list keeps everything chosen, and the sheet is withheld entirely when nothing chosen can go on one. Two smaller things had to move first. The save control took a selection object from one of the two mechanisms, which is what had kept it off the other; it takes characters now. And three surfaces worked out which member's page they were on by slicing the pathname by hand, which is one copy away from drifting - that is a shared hook.

name: One name for a search
summary: Every explorer takes the same parameter for a search now. There were four names for the one idea - the grade explorer used q, and the WaniKani, JLPT and study explorers each had their own - and the shared search bar coped by writing all three legacy names on every submit and reading whichever one matched the surface it happened to be on. Nothing was broken by it. What it cost was guessability: the address for finding a character depended on which explorer you were standing in, so no link to a search could be worked out without reading the code first, and the search results had to hardcode a different query for each destination. It is q everywhere, which is what a reader expects and what one explorer already used. Links and bookmarks already sent to people keep working - the old three are still read - but nothing writes them any more, so they drain out of circulation instead of being carried forever. A test holds the line: no file may spell one of those parameters for itself again.

name: The glyph is text too
summary: Splitting the subject colours into a brand weight and a darker text weight fixed the pills, where a colour carries ten-pixel uppercase, and left the other half untouched: the character itself, drawn in the brand colour at twenty-four pixels and up. WCAG asks 3:1 there rather than 4.5, and radical cyan reached 2.41:1 on white - so the pill reading RADICAL was legible while the 水 beside it was not. Radical is the only hue that moved, darkened by the least that clears the floor, and the dark theme keeps the original because on that ground it is the readable one at 7.06:1. Kanji and vocabulary were already above the line and are untouched, so the site still looks like itself. The pill ink moved a shade with it, since the tint it sits on is mixed from the brand colour and had darkened underneath it.

name: Articles, kept where the work is
summary: Written notes on what changed and why were being handed over as links to pages hosted elsewhere, which put them outside the repository, outside admin and outside version control - three places they belong. Admin now has an Articles tab: an index of pieces newest first with their length, and a reading page for each at a width prose is comfortable at. An article is a component in the same folder rather than a markdown file, because the site has no markdown renderer and adding a dependency to read four internal notes is a dependency for nothing, while a component inherits the site's own type, spacing and colour and cannot drift from them. The prose vocabulary is fixed - a lead, headings, points, figures, a release row and a note - so an article cannot quietly invent its own styling, and the list is a single registry, because an article that is not in it does not exist. The first piece is the write-up of the search rebuild and the two corpora that shipped alongside it.

name: The grade lives in the path
summary: John asked for explorer addresses that make sense, and the search half of that shipped already: every explorer reads q. This is the other half, starting with the grades. The grade moved out of the query and into the path - /grades/3 rather than /grades?grade=3 - because it says which collection is being looked at, which is what a link means to whoever receives it, and it is what a cache can key on. Searching and paging stay in the query, since they describe how a collection is being read rather than which one it is. Links already sent still work: the old address redirects to the new one carrying the search and page with it, and results built before the change land where they should. A segment that names no grade now returns a 404 rather than quietly rendering grade one, so a wrong link stops looking like a working one, and the writing-practice route beneath the same folder is untouched. The other two explorers follow this shape next.

name: One address, no shims
summary: The grades explorer shipped its path move with a redirect from the old query-string address, on the assumption that links already sent had to keep working. They do not: the site has no users yet, and a compatibility layer for links nobody sent is a second code path to understand, test and eventually remove in exchange for nothing. The redirect is gone, the collection root simply opens on the first grade because that is where the navigation points, and there is exactly one address for a grade. The rule is now in AGENTS.md so it is not relearned: change the thing and update every caller, with two exceptions where data outlives code - persisted database values like the revenge enum member and the batchSize sentinel, and anything already written to production, which needs migrating rather than shimming.

name: Practice is not a page under grades
summary: Writing practice lived at /grades/practice, which read as though the grades explorer owned it. It never did: it builds sheets from school grades, WaniKani levels, JLPT levels, either tagged list, or a set picked by hand on any surface. It is the thing you do to a collection rather than a page belonging to one of them, and filing it under one made the other four look like guests. It is a surface of its own now, at /practice, with the collection in the path - /practice/jlpt/5, /practice/grade/2, /practice/trouble - and how the sheet prints staying in the query, because that is how you are practising rather than what. A bare /practice opens the chooser, which is the point of it being top level: it is where you decide what to practise. A level on a list, or a source that does not exist, returns a 404 rather than a default sheet. The Back to grades button went with the move, since practice is no longer somewhere you arrive from grades, and the navigation now lists Practice beside the explorers rather than beneath one.

name: The card is not a button
summary: Every subject on an explorer sat inside one big control. The card was a button, and it holds buttons of its own - trouble, favourite, and the tick that chooses it - which is a control inside a control on four hundred and twenty-eight of them, one for every card on every list. What that costs is not theoretical. A screen reader announces the whole card as a single button and never reaches the favourite inside it, so the only way to mark a character as trouble is to see it. A keyboard arrives at the card and finds no way in. The glyph is the button now and the card is a plain container around it, which is the shape the saved lists and the history rows already used, so this is the odd one out being brought into line rather than a new idea. The controls at the glyph's foot are its neighbours instead of its children - the same corners, the same placement, nothing moved on screen - and each is reached, announced and pressed on its own. A whole card still answers a mouse click where it did before, because that is worth keeping and costs nothing once it is no longer the only way in.

name: All levels means all levels
summary: The WaniKani explorer offered a tab reading All with the total beside it - two thousand nine hundred and twenty-two - and pressing it did nothing you could see. It put the member back on their own level, which was the level already showing, so the list did not change, the address kept the same single level in it, and the number on the tab described a view nothing in the app could open. There was no way to look across every level at all. It selects every level now and fetches the ones it does not already hold, a few at a time rather than all at once, because a level that is not cached goes out to WaniKani and sixty of those together is how an account gets rate limited. Results widen as each batch lands instead of waiting for the last. The address carries the whole selection, so the long view is a link somebody can be sent. The subtitle went with it: it read Select one level at a time, which was true of nothing - Sticky has always let a member gather several - and it was the last thing still saying one.

name: A limit on signing up
summary: The route that creates an account had nothing bounding how often it could be called. It was never as bad as it sounds - a Google session is required before it does anything, and an address that already has an account gets that account back rather than a second one, so the ceiling was always one account per address rather than one per request. What was unbounded was the work behind it. Every call reads the signup settings, looks up the account, and scans every slug on the site to pick a free address, and a signed-in caller could repeat all of that as fast as they liked. Six attempts in ten minutes now, which leaves room for a form submitted twice, a retried request and a reload, and stops a loop. It is counted against the signed-in address rather than the caller's network address, because a household shares one of those - this one does - and a per-network budget would have the second person in a family turned away by the first. The check sits above all three reads rather than beside them, since a limit applied after the work bounds the answer and not the cost. None of this matters while the door is shut; all of it matters the moment it opens.
